newsitem.title: CHINA: Record volume seen on China domestic share markets.
newsitem.headline: Record volume seen on China domestic share markets.

text.p: China's domestic A share markets have surged in the past week with daily turnover also hitting their highest levels since the country's two stock exchanges were set up in 1990, analysts said on Thursday.

They said more and more investors were trading stocks on the exchanges in Shanghai and Shenzhen due to falling interest rates, an improved national economy and promises from Beijing to expand the markets.

On Thursday, the Shanghai A share index closed up 2.02 percent to 1001.727 points, a rise of 6.19 percent from the close on Wednesday last week. Its Shenzhen counterpart rose 8.58 percent to 375.59 points, a surge of 23.81 percent.
The indices are at their highest levels for two years.
Combined A share turnover on the two bourses has topped 20 billion yuan ($2.41 billion) a day for the past five trading days, with the highest on Monday at 22.8 billion yuan.
The turnover is bigger than at any time since China revived its stock markets in the early 1990s. The previous record volume was around 15 billion yuan a day in August 1994.
Before the current surge, normal daily volume was around five billion yuan, analysts said.
"Many new investors have turned to the stock markets this year after the two bank interest rate cuts," said a trader with J and A Securities.
"Funds which flowed out of the market during the two-year depression starting early 1994 have returned," said a stock analyst with China Guotai Securities.
"The crackdown on the futures markets has also pushed (speculative) hot money into the markets," he added.
The People's Bank of China, the central bank, cut bank interest rates in May and August on the back of falling inflation.
A Shanghai exchange official said on Thursday that a huge increase in new stock accounts had been seen since May with more than two million new accounts opened on the bourse so far this year.

In recent months, senior Chinese officials have repeatedly stressed Beijing's support for the stock markets, a significant turn-around from the previous official attitude, that the markets were an experiment.
Analysts said Beijing wanted to boost the markets to prepare them for greater competition with Hong Kong after it is handed over to China in the middle of next year.
Shanghai's A share market has risen around 70 percent in a bull run since mid-April and its Shenzhen counterpart more than 160 percent.
